summary.text: For consecutive primes \(p<q\), Wilson’s theorem and \((q-1)!=p!\bigl(\prod_{j=p+1}^{q-2}j\bigr)(q-1)\) show that \(p!\equiv1\pmod q\) exactly when the intervening product is \(1\pmod q\). If \(q=p+2\) this product is empty, while otherwise the gap exceeds two; a finite prime count identifies the exceptional pair as \((7841,7853)\), and direct modular multiplication gives the required product congruence there.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
2=p_1<p_2<p_3<\cdots
\]
denote the primes in increasing order. For a positive integer \(n\), the sequence \(a(n)\) is the increasing enumeration of the primes \(p\) for which \(p+2\) is also prime. Thus, for a prime \(p\), saying that \(p=a(n)\) for some \(n\) is equivalent to saying that \(p+2\) is prime: these are exactly the smaller members of twin-prime pairs. (For the forward direction, this is immediate from the definition of the enumeration; for the reverse direction, rank \(p\) among the finitely many qualifying integers at most \(p\).)

Fix \(k>1\), and write
\[
r=p_k,\qquad q=p_{k+1},\qquad
W=\prod_{j=r+1}^{q-2}j.
\]
As usual, a product over an empty interval is defined to be \(1\). We prove
\[
r!\equiv1\pmod q
\]
if and only if at least one of the following holds:

1. \(r+2\) is prime (equivalently, \(r=a(n)\) for some \(n\));
2. \(k=991\);
3. \(q-r>2\) and \(W\equiv1\pmod q\).

The central observation is the following consequence of Wilson's theorem.

**Wilson reduction.** If \(q\) is prime and \(r+2\le q\), then
\[
r!\equiv1\pmod q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\prod_{j=r+1}^{q-2}j\equiv1\pmod q.
\]

Indeed, split \((q-1)!\) into three consecutive parts:
\[
(q-1)!=r!\left(\prod_{j=r+1}^{q-2}j\right)(q-1)=r!W(q-1).
\]
Wilson's theorem says that \((q-1)!\equiv-1\pmod q\), while of course \(q-1\equiv-1\pmod q\). Hence
\[
-1\equiv-r!W\pmod q,
\]
and therefore
\[
r!W\equiv1\pmod q. \tag{1}
\]
If \(r!\equiv1\), equation (1) gives \(W\equiv1\); conversely, if \(W\equiv1\), equation (1) gives \(r!\equiv1\). This proves the reduction. For completeness, Wilson's theorem itself follows by pairing every nonzero residue modulo the prime \(q\) with its multiplicative inverse. The only residues equal to their own inverses are \(1\) and \(-1\), so the product of all nonzero residues is \(-1\).

We now verify that the reduction applies to \(r=p_k\) and \(q=p_{k+1}\). Since \(k>1\), we have \(r\ge p_2=3\). Thus \(r\) is an odd prime. The next integer \(r+1\) is even and exceeds \(2\), so it is not prime. Since \(q\) is the first prime after \(r\), it follows that
\[
q\ge r+2. \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, the Wilson reduction gives the fundamental equivalence
\[
r!\equiv1\pmod q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad W\equiv1\pmod q. \tag{3}
\]

We also need the numerical information at the stated exceptional index. We record both the computation and why the finite test used in it is sufficient.

For every integer \(n<7921=89^2\), \(n\) is prime if and only if \(n\ge2\) and no integer \(d\) with
\[
2\le d<89,\qquad d<n
\]
divides \(n\). One implication is immediate because a prime has no proper divisor at least \(2\). Conversely, if \(n\) is composite, write \(n=ab\) with \(a,b\ge2\), choosing \(a\le b\). Then \(a^2\le n<89^2\), so \(a<89\), and \(a\) is one of the divisors tested.

Thus primality of every integer below \(7921\) can be decided by trial division by the integers \(2,3,\ldots,88\). Applying this finite sieve to the intervals in question gives
\[
\#\{p:p\text{ prime and }p<7841\}=990,
\]
\[
\#\{p:p\text{ prime and }p<7853\}=991,
\]
and the same divisor test shows that both \(7841\) and \(7853\) are prime. One completely explicit way to perform the tally is to start with \(C(0)=0\) and, for each \(N<7921\), set
\[
C(N+1)=
\begin{cases}
C(N)+1,&N\ge2\text{ and no }d\in\{2,\ldots,88\}\text{ divides }N,\\
C(N),&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The exhaustive tally gives \(C(7841)=990\) and \(C(7853)=991\). Since each endpoint is itself prime, these counts identify its zero-based rank among the primes. Equivalently,
\[
p_{991}=7841,\qquad p_{992}=7853. \tag{4}
\]
As a local check that there is no prime strictly between these two endpoints, the intervening integers have the following evident proper divisors:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccccc}
n&7842&7843&7844&7845&7846&7847&7848&7849&7850&7851&7852\\ \hline
\text{divisor}&2&11&2&3&2&7&2&47&2&3&2.
\end{array}
\]
The global sieve count below \(7841\), rather than merely this local check, is what identifies the index as \(991\).

At \(k=991\), equations (4) give \(r=7841\) and \(q=7853\). The relevant product can be evaluated particularly simply modulo \(7853\):
\[
W=\prod_{j=7842}^{7851}j
\equiv(-11)(-10)\cdots(-2)\pmod{7853}.
\]
There are ten negative factors, so
\[
W\equiv 11\cdot10\cdots2=11!=39916800.
\]
But
\[
39916800=7853\cdot5083+1,
\]
and hence
\[
W\equiv1\pmod{7853}. \tag{5}
\]
This establishes the modular fact needed for the exceptional disjunct.

We now prove the two directions of the claimed equivalence.

Suppose first that
\[
r!\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
By (3), \(W\equiv1\pmod q\). There are two cases.

If \(r+2\) is prime, then \(r\) is the smaller member of a twin-prime pair, so \(r=a(n)\) for some \(n\). The first disjunct holds.

If \(r+2\) is not prime, then \(q\ne r+2\), because \(q\) is prime. Together with (2), this gives \(q>r+2\), or equivalently
\[
q-r>2.
\]
We already know that \(W\equiv1\pmod q\), so the third disjunct holds. This proves the forward implication. Notice that this direction does not need to single out \(k=991\): if that index occurs, it also satisfies the long-gap product condition.

Conversely, suppose that one of the three stated alternatives holds.

First assume that \(r+2\) is prime. Since \(q\) is the next prime after \(r\), the existence of the prime \(r+2\) implies \(q\le r+2\). Combining this with (2) yields
\[
q=r+2.
\]
Therefore
\[
W=\prod_{j=r+1}^{q-2}j
 =\prod_{j=r+1}^{r}j=1,
\]
because the indexing interval is empty. Hence \(W\equiv1\pmod q\), and (3) gives \(r!\equiv1\pmod q\).

Next assume that \(k=991\). Then (4) identifies \((r,q)=(7841,7853)\), and (5) gives \(W\equiv1\pmod q\). Again (3) gives
\[
r!\equiv1\pmod q.
\]

Finally, assume that \(q-r>2\) and \(W\equiv1\pmod q\). The second part of this assumption, together with (3), immediately yields
\[
r!\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
(The gap inequality identifies this as a non-twin case but is not otherwise needed once the product congruence has been supplied.)

All three reverse cases therefore imply the factorial congruence, completing the equivalence for every \(k>1\).
